title: Electromotive force and voltage
summary: Explains electromotive force (emf) and potential difference (pd), how they differ, sources of emf, and how pd relates to voltage drop in series circuits.

sections.heading: Electromotive force (emf)
paragraphs: Applying an electrical charge across a conductor causes a current to flow. For electrons to move, the charge must apply a force. This force is the electromotive force (emf), measured in volts, and a battery is an example of a source of emf.

If the emf is increased, the current increases. When the emf is removed, the current stops because of the electrical resistance in the conductor. Because electrons have moved, work must have been done.
bullets: If the rate of doing work is 1 watt when the current is 1 ampere, the applied emf is 1 volt (1 V)

sections.heading: Sources of emf
paragraphs: There are five sources of electromotive force.

sections.heading: Potential difference (pd)
paragraphs: Resistance in the conductor opposes the flow of current, so the force acting on the electrons is different between any two points along the conductor. This difference is the potential difference (pd), measured in volts. When 1 ampere dissipates 1 watt, the pd is 1 volt.

In a simple circuit with a 2 V battery and no wire resistance, the pd across the lamp is 2 V. Wires always have some resistance: if each wire has a pd of 0.5 V, the pd across the lamp becomes 1 V, so the lamp is not as bright.
bullets: emf causes electric current to flow
pd is caused by the flow of electric current
As electrons pass through the lamp, the resistance of the filament makes them lose energy; this loss is the pd

sections.heading: Voltage drop
paragraphs: In any series circuit, the sum of the pds always equals the applied emf. In practice, pd is often called voltage drop. Cables have resistance, so volt drop occurs along them, and this is an important factor in designing electrical installations.
bullets: Series circuit: sum of the pds = applied emf
Potential difference is often referred to as voltage drop
Volt drop along cables must be taken into account when designing installations

flashcards.back: The force applied by a charge that makes electrons move and current flow in a conductor, measured in volts.

flashcards.front: Give an example of a source of emf.
What happens to current if the emf is increased?
Why does current stop when emf is removed?
flashcards.back: Because of the electrical resistance in the conductor.

flashcards.front: When is the applied emf 1 volt?
flashcards.back: When the rate of doing work is 1 watt with a current of 1 ampere.

flashcards.front: List the five sources of emf.
flashcards.back: Electromagnetic induction, electrochemical, photoelectric effect, thermoelectric effect and piezoelectric effect.
The difference in the force acting on electrons between two points along a conductor, caused by resistance. Measured in volts.

flashcards.front: How do emf and pd differ in cause and effect?
flashcards.back: emf causes electric current to flow; pd is caused by the flow of electric current.

flashcards.front: What is the rule for pds in a series circuit?
flashcards.back: The sum of the pds always equals the applied emf.
In practice, another name for potential difference, such as the volt drop along cables because of their resistance.

flashcards.front: Why does volt drop matter in installations?
flashcards.back: Cables have resistance, so volt drop occurs along them and must be considered when designing electrical installations.

quiz.q: In which unit is electromotive force measured?
Which of these is a source of emf?
quiz.why: Sources include electromagnetic induction, electrochemical, photoelectric, thermoelectric and piezoelectric effects.

options: pd causes current to flow; emf is caused by current
emf causes current to flow; pd is caused by the flow of current
emf and pd are both caused by resistance only
pd is a source of electromotive force
quiz.why: emf causes electric current to flow and pd is caused by the flow of electric current.

quiz.q: A 2 V battery supplies a lamp through wires with no resistance. What is the pd across the lamp?
quiz.why: Assuming the wires have no resistance, the pd across the lamp is 2 V.

quiz.q: A 2 V battery supplies a lamp through two wires, each with a pd of 0.5 V. What is the pd across the lamp?
quiz.why: In a series circuit the pds add up to the emf, so 2 V - 0.5 V - 0.5 V leaves 1 V across the lamp.

quiz.q: What happens to the brightness of the lamp when the wire resistance is included?
quiz.why: The pd across the lamp drops to 1 V, so the lamp will not be as bright.

quiz.q: In any series circuit, the sum of the pds equals what?
quiz.why: In any series circuit the sum of the pds always equals the applied emf.

quiz.q: What is potential difference often called in practice?
quiz.why: In practice, potential difference is often referred to as voltage drop.

quiz.q: What happens to the current when the emf is removed from a conductor?
quiz.why: As soon as the emf is removed the current stops due to the resistance in the conductor.
